title: Controllers and REST design
intro: A Spring Boot controller is the part of your backend that turns HTTP requests into Java method calls and Java results into HTTP responses. In this lesson, you will design a clean REST API for the task manager and learn how controllers handle paths, query parameters, request bodies, status codes and headers.
body:
## Think in resources, not actions

A REST API exposes **resources** through URLs. A resource is a thing your application manages, such as a task, user, booking or product.

~~~diagram
{"type": "layers", "title": "Resources and verbs", "caption": "Nouns in the URL, verbs in the HTTP method.", "layers": [{"label": "GET /api/tasks", "sub": "list → 200", "items": ["?done=false&page=0"]}, {"label": "GET /api/tasks/42", "sub": "one → 200 or 404"}, {"label": "POST /api/tasks", "sub": "create → 201 + Location", "highlight": true}, {"label": "PUT /api/tasks/42", "sub": "replace → 200"}, {"label": "PATCH /api/tasks/42", "sub": "partial update → 200"}, {"label": "DELETE /api/tasks/42", "sub": "remove → 204"}]}
~~~

For our task manager, a task is a resource. A collection of tasks is represented by:

~~~text
/api/tasks
~~~

A single task is represented by:

~~~text
/api/tasks/42
~~~

Notice that the URL uses nouns rather than verbs. You generally do not need URLs such as `/api/getTasks` or `/api/createTask`. The HTTP method already describes the operation.

This gives us a predictable API:

| HTTP method | URL | Meaning | Typical response |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET | `/api/tasks` | List tasks | 200 OK |
| GET | `/api/tasks/42` | Get one task | 200 OK or 404 Not Found |
| POST | `/api/tasks` | Create a task | 201 Created + Location |
| PUT | `/api/tasks/42` | Replace a task | 200 OK |
| PATCH | `/api/tasks/42` | Partially update a task | 200 OK |
| DELETE | `/api/tasks/42` | Delete a task | 204 No Content |

These conventions make the API easier for your React frontend and other clients to understand.

## HTTP methods and status codes

HTTP status codes communicate what happened with a request. The response body can contain useful data, but the status code is an important part of the API contract.

A successful GET commonly returns `200 OK`.

When a POST creates a new resource, return `201 Created`. A useful REST API also includes a `Location` header containing the URL of the new resource.

For example:

~~~text
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /api/tasks/42
~~~

A successful DELETE can return `204 No Content`. This tells the client that the operation succeeded and there is intentionally no response body.

For client errors, `400 Bad Request` means the request itself is invalid. We will cover detailed validation errors in the next lesson.

`404 Not Found` means the requested resource does not exist.

`409 Conflict` is useful when the request conflicts with the current state of the resource. For example, you might use it when trying to create a resource that violates a uniqueness rule.

You can read more about HTTP methods and status codes in [MDN's HTTP documentation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP).

## Create a controller

Spring provides the `@RestController` annotation for HTTP API controllers.

~~~java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/tasks")
public class TaskController {
}
~~~

`@RestController` tells Spring that this class handles web requests and that its return values should normally become HTTP response bodies.

`@RequestMapping` defines a common path for the controller. Every mapping inside this class can therefore start with `/api/tasks`.

A controller should normally deal with HTTP concerns: reading request data, selecting the appropriate operation and creating the response. Business rules and database operations will eventually move into other layers.

## GET endpoints

To return all tasks, use `@GetMapping`:

~~~java
@GetMapping
public List<TaskResponse> list() {
    return taskService.findAll();
}
~~~

Spring maps a GET request to `/api/tasks` to this method.

For one task, use a path variable:

~~~java
@GetMapping("/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<TaskResponse> get(@PathVariable Long id) {
    return taskService.findById(id)
        .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
        .orElseGet(() -> ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
}
~~~

`@PathVariable` reads a value from the URL. For `/api/tasks/42`, the `id` parameter receives `42`.

The `{id}` part of the mapping and the `@PathVariable Long id` parameter work together.

## Query parameters for filters

Not every piece of input belongs in the path. Query parameters are useful for optional filters, sorting and pagination.

For example:

~~~text
GET /api/tasks?done=true
~~~

The controller can read the value with `@RequestParam`:

~~~java
@GetMapping
public List<TaskResponse> list(
    @RequestParam(required = false) Boolean done
) {
    return taskService.findAll(done);
}
~~~

`required = false` means the parameter is optional. Without it, Spring expects the parameter to be present.

Pagination can use the same approach:

~~~text
GET /api/tasks?page=0&size=20
~~~

~~~java
@GetMapping
public List<TaskResponse> list(
    @RequestParam(required = false) Boolean done,
    @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,
    @RequestParam(defaultValue = "20") int size
) {
    return taskService.findAll(done, page, size);
}
~~~

This keeps the resource URL stable while allowing the client to request a particular view of the collection.

## POST and request bodies

A POST request usually contains data in its request body. In JSON, creating a task might look like this:

~~~json
{
  "title": "Learn Spring Boot"
}
~~~

Spring can convert this JSON into a Java object using `@RequestBody`.

A record is a convenient DTO for this purpose:

~~~java
public record CreateTaskRequest(String title) {}
~~~

A **DTO (Data Transfer Object)** is an object designed specifically for data moving into or out of an API. It is not necessarily the same object you use internally or for database persistence.

The controller can then look like this:

~~~java
@PostMapping
public ResponseEntity<TaskResponse> create(
    @RequestBody CreateTaskRequest request
) {
    TaskResponse task = taskService.create(request);

    return ResponseEntity
        .created(URI.create("/api/tasks/" + task.id()))
        .body(task);
}
~~~

`@RequestBody` tells Spring to deserialize the JSON request body into the specified Java type.

The `created(...)` response builder sets the `201 Created` status and the `Location` header. `.body(...)` supplies the response body.

## PUT, PATCH and DELETE

Use `PUT` when the client is replacing the resource representation.

~~~java
@PutMapping("/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<TaskResponse> update(
    @PathVariable Long id,
    @RequestBody UpdateTaskRequest request
) {
    // update the task
}
~~~

`PATCH` is useful for partial updates. For example, the React application might only want to change `done`:

~~~json
{
  "done": true
}
~~~

The controller can expose this with:

~~~java
@PatchMapping("/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<TaskResponse> patch(
    @PathVariable Long id,
    @RequestBody UpdateTaskRequest request
) {
    // partially update the task
}
~~~

For deletion:

~~~java
@DeleteMapping("/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<Void> remove(@PathVariable Long id) {
    taskService.delete(id);
    return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
}
~~~

`ResponseEntity<Void>` communicates that the response has no body. A successful deletion returns `204 No Content`.

## ResponseEntity gives you control

Sometimes returning an object directly is enough:

~~~java
@GetMapping
public List<TaskResponse> list() {
    return taskService.findAll();
}
~~~

Spring will normally return `200 OK` and serialise the list as JSON.

When you need to control the status code or headers, use `ResponseEntity`.

~~~java
return ResponseEntity
    .status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT)
    .body(errorResponse);
~~~

You can also set headers explicitly:

~~~java
return ResponseEntity
    .status(HttpStatus.CREATED)
    .header("Location", "/api/tasks/42")
    .body(task);
~~~

This is why `ResponseEntity` is useful for REST controllers: it represents the HTTP response rather than only the response body.

## Return DTOs, not entities

As we introduce a database, you will have JPA entities representing database records. It is tempting to return those entities directly from controllers.

~~~compare
{"left": {"title": "Returning the entity", "lang": "java", "code": "@GetMapping(\"/{id}\")\nUser get(@PathVariable long id) {\n  return repo.findById(id).orElseThrow();\n}\n// {\"id\":1,\"passwordHash\":\"$2a$…\"}", "note": "Leaks internal fields and ties the API to the table."}, "right": {"title": "Returning a DTO", "lang": "java", "code": "record UserResponse(long id, String name) {}\n\n@GetMapping(\"/{id}\")\nUserResponse get(@PathVariable long id) {\n  return service.find(id);\n}", "note": "The API shape is a deliberate contract."}}
~~~

Avoid making that the default design.

A database entity describes persistence. A DTO describes your API contract. Keeping them separate means you can change your database model without automatically changing the JSON API.

For example:

~~~java
public record TaskResponse(
    Long id,
    String title,
    boolean done
) {}
~~~

The controller returns `TaskResponse`, not `TaskEntity`.

This separation also helps prevent accidentally exposing fields that should remain internal.

## JSON and Jackson

Spring Boot's web starter includes Jackson, a library that converts Java objects to and from JSON.

This process has two common directions:

~~~text
JSON request
    ↓
Jackson deserialisation
    ↓
Java DTO

Java DTO
    ↓
Jackson serialisation
    ↓
JSON response
~~~

For example, this record:

~~~java
public record TaskResponse(Long id, String title, boolean done) {}
~~~

can become:

~~~json
{
  "id": 1,
  "title": "Learn Spring Boot",
  "done": false
}
~~~

You normally do not need to manually construct JSON strings in a Spring controller.

## Test the API with curl

IntelliJ IDEA's built-in HTTP client is available in IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate, so it is not part of the Community Edition workflow we use in this course.

For simple API testing, `curl` is enough.

Get all tasks:

~~~shell
curl http://localhost:8080/api/tasks
~~~

Get one task:

~~~shell
curl http://localhost:8080/api/tasks/1
~~~

Create a task:

~~~shell
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/tasks \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"Learn REST controllers"}'
~~~

You can also use Postman if you prefer a graphical API client. The important thing is that you can send requests and inspect status codes, headers and JSON responses independently of React.

## CORS and the React development server

During development, your React frontend and Spring Boot backend may run on different origins. For example, Vite might run on `http://localhost:5173` while Spring Boot runs on `http://localhost:8080`.

~~~diagram
{"type": "sequence", "title": "A CORS preflight", "actors": ["Browser :5173", "API :8080"], "steps": [{"from": "Browser :5173", "to": "API :8080", "label": "OPTIONS /api/tasks (Origin: localhost:5173)"}, {"from": "API :8080", "to": "Browser :5173", "label": "Access-Control-Allow-Origin: localhost:5173", "dashed": true}, {"from": "Browser :5173", "to": "API :8080", "label": "POST /api/tasks"}, {"from": "API :8080", "to": "Browser :5173", "label": "201 Created", "dashed": true}]}
~~~

The browser's **CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)** rules can block frontend requests between different origins unless the backend explicitly allows them.

For a small development setup, you can allow the React development server on a controller:

~~~java
@CrossOrigin(origins = "http://localhost:5173")
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/tasks")
public class TaskController {
}
~~~

For a larger application, configure CORS centrally with `WebMvcConfigurer` instead of repeating the annotation on many controllers.

~~~java
@Configuration
public class WebConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {

    @Override
    public void addCorsMappings(CorsRegistry registry) {
        registry.addMapping("/api/**")
            .allowedOrigins("http://localhost:5173")
            .allowedMethods("GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE");
    }
}
~~~

Do not blindly allow every origin in production. CORS is a browser security mechanism, so your production configuration should explicitly allow the frontend origins that should access the API.

## API versioning

When an API contract needs a breaking change, you can introduce a version such as `/api/v1/tasks` and `/api/v2/tasks` so clients can migrate without being broken immediately. Versioning strategies differ, but the important principle is to treat your API contract as something clients depend on.

## Common mistakes

### Using verbs in resource URLs

Prefer `/api/tasks` with POST over `/api/createTask`. The HTTP method already communicates the operation.

### Returning 200 for everything

Status codes are part of the API contract. Use `201` when a resource is created, `204` for a successful response with no body, and `404` when the requested resource does not exist.

### Returning database entities directly

Entities are persistence models. DTOs are API models. Keeping them separate gives you more control over your public API.

### Forgetting the Location header

When creating a resource with POST, `201 Created` together with a `Location` header tells the client where the newly created resource can be retrieved.

### Putting validation into this controller too early

For this lesson, focus on REST mapping and response design. The next lesson will introduce request validation and consistent error responses.

### Allowing every CORS origin in production

A permissive development configuration may be convenient locally, but production should allow only the origins that actually need access.

## The controller's role

Your controller is the HTTP boundary of the application. It receives HTTP data, converts it into DTOs, calls application logic and creates an HTTP response.

For the task manager, the flow will eventually look like this:

~~~text
React
  ↓ HTTP
TaskController
  ↓
TaskService
  ↓
TaskRepository
  ↓
PostgreSQL
~~~

The controller should not contain all the business logic. In the next lesson, you will add validation so that requests such as an empty task title can be rejected consistently with a useful `400 Bad Request` response.
takeaways: REST APIs represent resources with noun-based URLs and use HTTP methods to describe operations.
Spring controllers map HTTP methods and URL parameters to Java methods with annotations such as @GetMapping and @PostMapping.
ResponseEntity lets you control HTTP status codes, headers and response bodies.
DTOs keep the API contract separate from database entities and internal application models.
CORS controls which browser origins can call your API, while curl and Postman let you test the backend independently of React.

quiz.question: Which URL best represents the collection of tasks in a REST API?
quiz.explanation: REST APIs normally represent resources with nouns. The tasks collection is naturally represented by /api/tasks.

quiz.question: What status code is normally appropriate when a POST request successfully creates a new task?
quiz.explanation: A successful resource creation normally returns 201 Created. A Location header can identify the newly created resource.

options: A value from the JSON request body
The value represented by {id} in the URL
A value from an environment variable
quiz.explanation: @PathVariable binds a value from a URI template such as /api/tasks/42 to the Java method parameter.

quiz.question:
What does this request do?

GET /api/tasks?done=true
options: Requests a task whose ID is true
Requests tasks filtered by the done query parameter
quiz.explanation: The done=true part is a query parameter. A controller can use @RequestParam to read it and filter the task collection.

quiz.question: Which response is appropriate when DELETE successfully removes a task and there is no response body?
options: 200 OK with an empty JSON object
quiz.explanation: 204 No Content communicates that the operation succeeded and intentionally has no response body.

exercise.title: Mirror a Spring REST controller
exercise.task: Write a TypeScript class called TaskController that mirrors the design of a Spring REST controller. Keep an in-memory list of tasks inside the controller, with IDs starting at 1. Every method must return an object shaped like a ResponseEntity: { status, headers?, body }. Implement list(query?: { done?: boolean }) to return status 200 and all tasks, filtering by done when the value is provided. Implement get(id) to return status 200 with the matching task, or status 404 with body { error: "Task not found" }. Implement create(dto: { title: string }) to create a task with the next ID, the supplied title and done: false, returning status 201, the new task as the body, and a Location header whose value is "/api/tasks/<id>". Implement update(id, dto: { title?: string; done?: boolean }) to update only the supplied fields and return status 200 with the updated task, or 404 when the task does not exist. Implement remove(id) to delete the task and return status 204 with body null, or 404 when it does not exist. Do not add validation yet; validation is the subject of the next lesson. This TypeScript class mirrors the Java/Spring controller design you will build in IntelliJ IDEA in the full sample project.
exercise.hint: Use find() for get() and update(), and findIndex() plus splice() for remove(). For list(), only filter when query?.done is actually defined. In create(), increment nextId after assigning it. In update(), check each optional property against undefined so that only supplied fields change.
